provenance: Authored against the sponsor's BDM scope (CAR-T for LN, CAR-T for MS, Long-Term Follow-Up). The MS questions are reframed from the LN set to land MS-specific friction: DMT identity, relapse anxiety, neurologist-of-record continuity, and disability progression measurement at home.

section.headline: Four LTFU questions tuned to MS-specific retention risk.
section.body: MS patients carry a different LTFU profile than LN: a stronger DMT identity, sharper relapse anxiety, and a community neurologist who often outranks the trial site as the trusted voice. The questions below frame LTFU operational levers that hold up under those conditions.

questions.label: What would make a CAR-T MS patient feel safe enough to stay off their DMT for 12 years?
questions.summary: MS DMT identity is durable — patients have spent years optimizing their DMT regimen. Even an MRI-quiet, relapse-free year does not by itself dislodge the anxiety. Without active reassurance work, DMT restart at the first MRI surprise will be the default.

research.headline: Questions to ask or source from patients
items: What would the patient need to see at year 1, year 3, year 5 to feel safe staying off DMT?
Whose voice is most persuasive when a stable MRI shows up — trial PI, community neurologist, online cohort, family?
What does the patient consider an acceptable rescue threshold (new lesion, clinical symptom, MRI activity) before restarting DMT?
What language does the patient use to describe being off-DMT — cured, in remission, between regimens?

items.label: DMT-restart guardrail protocol
items.body: Equivalent to the LN rescue-immunosuppression flag, but tuned to MS DMT classes. Triggers a structured ascertainment workflow on any new DMT prescription, with a community-neurologist outreach loop that pre-empts confounding restarts.

items.label: Cohort-anchored reassurance dashboard
items.body: Patient-facing cohort-level view of stable MRI, relapse-free intervals, and disability scores across the trial population at each year mark. Earns the patient's confidence that staying off DMT is not an outlier choice.

questions.label: How does relapse anxiety reshape LTFU engagement year over year?
questions.summary: MS engagement curves do not decay smoothly. Spikes track to symptom episodes, MRI dates, and DMT-renewal anniversaries. A flat LTFU cadence misses the moments when patients most want to be heard — and the moments when they most want to disappear.

research.headline: Questions to ask or source from patients
items: What new symptom would make the patient reach out vs hide from the trial site?
What does the patient want the trial site to do if an MRI shows a quiet new lesion that they did not feel?
When does the LTFU contact feel like reassurance vs intrusion?
Which channels does the patient prefer at calm vs anxious moments — text, portal, video, written letter?

items.label: Anxiety-aware contact cadence
items.body: Vary outreach cadence around expected anxiety peaks (annual MRI weeks, DMT-restart-anniversary windows). Uses ePRO sentiment trigger to surface a check-in when patient-reported anxiety jumps.

items.label: Two-way symptom-report channel
items.body: Patient-initiated symptom report with a same-business-day response SLA. Captures the in-between-visit episodes that drive payor questions about durability of disease control, and removes the silent-dropout risk.

questions.label: What community-neurologist handoffs preserve protocol fidelity for 12 years?
questions.summary: MS patients tend to anchor more on their community MS-specialist neurologist than on the trial site, especially after year 2. If the community provider does not see themselves as a partner in the LTFU thesis, retention will bleed through provider-driven decisions (DMT restart, referral attrition, off-protocol MRI cadence).

research.headline: Questions to ask or source from patients
items: Who is the patient's call-first MS provider at year 1, year 5, year 10? Where does the trial site sit in that hierarchy?
What does the community neurologist need to take ownership of CAR-T LTFU data, not just sign annual forms?
What language does the trial team need to use with the community provider to align rather than threaten ownership?
What happens at the first community-side provider rotation (group practice churn, retirement)?

items.label: Community-neurologist transition bundle
items.body: Author a transition kit specifically for community MS specialists: 12-year data thesis, MRI cadence protocol that preserves study comparability, relapse-management decision tree that does not confound efficacy data, and a named coordinator contact.

items.label: Joint LTFU progress notes
items.body: Quarterly joint progress note signed by trial coordinator and community neurologist. Builds a shared record that survives PI rotation on the trial side and provider churn on the community side.

questions.label: Which PROs capture MS disability progression at home with low burden?
questions.summary: Payors will price MS CAR-T against years-of-disability-progression avoided and DMT-cycle costs offset. EDSS in clinic does not survive a digital-first LTFU framework. The instrument bank needs to be re-engineered for home capture without losing payor-grade signal.

research.headline: Questions to ask or source from patients
items: Which daily-function measures would the patient agree to capture quarterly from home for 12 years?
What does the patient consider a real change vs a bad-day artifact in fatigue, mobility, or cognition?
What burden ceiling (minutes per quarter) keeps PROs from being skipped or rushed?
Which life-event triggers (new job, pregnancy attempt, infection, surgery) does the patient see as worth a longitudinal data point?

items.label: Payor-aligned home ePRO bank
items.body: Curate a short MS-tuned ePRO bank — patient-reported MSIS-29 subscales, work-productivity, walking confidence, cognitive function — surfaced quarterly under a 5-minute burden ceiling. Generates the disability-progression-avoided narrative payors will demand.

items.label: Passive-signal validation study
items.body: Run a sub-study validating phone-passive signals (gait, typing cadence, sleep) against in-clinic disability scores. If passive signals hold up, years 5–12 can rely on near-zero patient effort while keeping the LTFU dataset payor-grade.
